messages.subject: Re: R 3.0 compatibility issues with R/qtl
parts:
I'm not exactly sure what's going on and what you should do.
Maybe try a different repository?

options(repos="http://cran.mtu.edu")
install.packages("qtl")

karl

messages.author: 5865ad824030260e
messages.subject: Qtl effect
parts:
Hi Karl,

I would like to calculate how much a QTL contributes to the phenotipic
variation observed. Can I use fitqtl even if I am just analysing one locus?

I tried and got (below) this results, but I am not sure if I can trust it
and, can I use the 86.29% variability?

Thanks a lot

Results:

fitqtl summary

Method: multiple imputation
Model: normal phenotype
Number of observations : 26

Full model result
----------------------------------
Model formula: y ~ Q1

df SS MS LOD %var Pvalue(Chi2) Pvalue(F)
Model 1 10530.111 10530.11081 11.22224 86.29905 6.531442e-13 7.545742e-12
Error 24 1671.774 69.65724
Total 25 12201.885


Estimated effects:
-----------------
est SE t
Intercept 23.899 1.642 14.56
4...@1164.4 40.369 3.283 12.29

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Qtl effect
parts:
Yes that's right. The estimate comes from transforming the LOD score, using the sample size.

You're right to not fully trust it; with a small sample, the estimate will have a large SE.

But I don't think I've seen a LOD score that big with a sample size of 26. I expect there is a large separation between the QTL genotypes, so saying the majority of variation is due to the QTL may be reasonable. I'd want to see a plot of phenotype vs genotype.

karl

Yes, looks reasonable. I'd consider taking logs or square root, or log(x+a) for some small a, to make the variation in the two groups more comparable. 

karl
